newsitem.title: ZAIRE: Refugees in Zaire die of thirst.
newsitem.headline: Refugees in Zaire die of thirst.

text.p: Rwandan refugees are dying of thirst in the harsh mountains of east Zaire, U.N. officials said on Thursday quoting some of the first eyewitness accounts from the war-ravaged region.
Refugees arriving in the Rwandan town of Gisenyi bordering on the Zairean city of Goma told U.N. officials of many deaths in the waterless, volcanic mountains north of Lake Kivu.

"They said they saw people dying all around them due to lack of water on the escarpment above Kahindo and Katale camps. One man was sucking water out of tree roots," said Peter Kessler, Nairobi spokesman of the U.N. High Commissioner for Refugees.
European Union aid ministers met in Brussels on Thursday to try to define a joint approach to the deepening tragedy, but there was a sharp divergence of views among aid organisations on what to do.
U.N. refugee chief Sadaka Ogata, in Brussels for the EU meeting, said the international community should send a "neutral force" empowered to arrest and disarm militias and other groups.
"I would like to see them empowered to do that, that should be one of their functions if such a force goes in," Ogata told Reuters.
Eastern Zaire is awash with arms, as a U.N. report made clear this week, and disarming the men with guns would be a tall order.
"Military intervention is not the answer in Zaire. It will take too long and, even if agreed, may well compound the problems in the region," the Save the Children Fund said.
Mark Bowden, the charity's east Africa director who has just returned from the region, said in London military protection was not necessary for the aid effort.
Aid agencies have been ringing alarm bells about the 1.2 million refugees in eastern Zaire for weeks, but efforts to help have so far faded before the sheer complexities of the task.
The part of east Zaire where the refugees are dying is no longer in government hands.
It is held by an extraordinary medley of armies and militias acting out tribal and political rivalries, fuelled by land hunger, which threaten to tear Zaire apart.
Most of the refugees are Rwandan Hutus who fled into Zaire after the Hutu genocide of up to one million Tutsis and other victims in Rwanda in 1994.
The rebels who captured much of eastern Zaire in a two-week lightning offensive include Tutsis, the Hutus' foes.

Many refugees fear that if they return to their countries of origin, Rwanda and Burundi, they will be slaughtered by Tutsi-led armies. Only about 2,000 Rwandan refugees have returned to Rwanda in recent weeks, U.N. officials say.
More than 20,000 Zairean refugees have fled the mayhem, U.N. officials said, and many have arrived wounded or exhausted in neighbouring countries.
Wendy Driscoll, a spokeswoman for CARE International in Nairobi, said the agency had reports of a 14 percent severe malnutrition rate among refugee children under five arriving in Tanzania.
On Wednesday Zairean President Mobutu Sese Seko gave his support for an international intervention force to go into eastern Zaire on a humanitarian mission.
Mobutu has warmed to a French plan for an intervention force, hoping perhaps that it might be a way to reassert his control in eastern Zaire.

Providing military help for Mobutu is not on the agenda of the United States, which has long barred him from its soil over his human rights record. Washington complains France is not being clear about what it envisages.
U.S. officials said the proposals were changing daily, creating confusion. Questions about what is a safe corridor and what troops might be involved have not been answered, they said.
On Wednesday the State Department said Washington was leaning toward backing the proposed force but would not itself contribute ground troops.
The slow pace of diplomacy means countless refugees are dying daily before any effective external help is provided.
The Organisation of African Unity plans no further meeting on Zaire until next Monday. Only France, Spain and Ethiopia have promised troops for an intervention force for eastern Zaire.

The U.N. special envoy on Zaire, Raymond Chretien, who met Mobutu on Wednesday, was due in Nairobi on Thursday before travelling to Rwanda on Friday. Rwanda is seen as a key player in the conflict since its government has sent forces into Zaire to back the Tutsi rebels.
In Goma, the biggest city under rebel control, rebels on Thursday supervised the distribution of oil, salt, biscuits and maize from a U.N. warehouse. Food in Goma is now scarce.
